reconstructed_theorem_text: For every natural number n ≥ 2, let E = ℝⁿ with its standard Euclidean inner product and norm, and define F: E → ℝ by F(x) = log ‖x‖ if n = 2 and F(x) = ‖x‖^(2 − n) otherwise, with the latter power interpreted as a real power. Then F is harmonic on a neighborhood of each point of E ∖ {0}: at every x ≠ 0, F is locally C² and its actual Euclidean Laplacian vanishes throughout some neighborhood of x. Moreover, for every real radius R > 0 and every x ∈ E satisfying ‖x‖ = R, both F(x) = log R if n = 2 and F(x) = R^(2 − n) if n ≥ 3, and ⟨∇F(x), R⁻¹x⟩ = R⁻¹ if n = 2 and ⟨∇F(x), R⁻¹x⟩ = (2 − n)R^(1 − n) if n ≥ 3. The gradient is the Riesz representative of the actual Fréchet derivative, and R⁻¹x is the outward radial unit vector on that sphere. Dimension expressions in real exponents and coefficients use the real value of n. No harmonicity, regularity, or sphere identity is asserted at the origin or for a nonpositive radius.
objects: n: a natural-number dimension; E = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n), namely standard real Euclidean n-space; F: E → ℝ, the dimension-dependent radial function log ‖x‖ for n = 2 and ‖x‖ raised to real exponent 2 − n otherwise; R: a real radius; x: a point of E. The gradient is the actual Fréchet gradient. Harmonicity uses the actual Euclidean Laplacian, the orthonormal trace of the actual second Fréchet derivative.
domains: F is defined as a total real-valued function on E by the displayed conditional and the real log/real-power operations. The harmonicity conclusion is restricted to E ∖ {0}. Sphere conclusions are restricted to R > 0 and ‖x‖ = R, so every norm occurring there is positive. There is no upper bound on R and no restriction to the unit ball. Dimensions zero and one are excluded by n ≥ 2.
quantifiers: For every n ∈ ℕ, assume 2 ≤ n and define F as displayed. Assert (i) harmonicity on neighborhoods of all nonzero points, and (ii) for every R ∈ ℝ, if 0 < R, then for every x ∈ E, if ‖x‖ = R, the boundary-value and radial-gradient identities both hold. The harmonicity conjunct is independent of the subsequently quantified radius.
assumptions: The sole dimension assumption is n ≥ 2. For each sphere statement there are additionally the assumptions R > 0 and ‖x‖ = R. No regularity premise is imposed on F: local C² regularity away from zero is part of the harmonicity conclusion. All inner products and norms are standard Euclidean ones.
conclusion: First, F satisfies InnerProductSpace.HarmonicOnNhd on {0}ᶜ, meaning local C² regularity and vanishing actual Laplacian on a neighborhood of every nonzero point. Second, on every positive-radius sphere, F(x) equals log R in dimension two and R^(2 − n) in dimensions n ≥ 3, and its gradient inner product with R⁻¹ • x equals R⁻¹ in dimension two and (2 − n) · R^(1 − n) in dimensions n ≥ 3. The two sphere identities are conjoined for each eligible R and x.
scopes: The dimension-two branch is selected by n = 2; under n ≥ 2 the other branch consists exactly of n ≥ 3. Harmonicity covers the entire punctured Euclidean space, locally around each of its points, with no assertion at zero. Sphere identities cover all points of every sphere centered at zero with strictly positive radius. They give the scalar radial component of ∇F, not an explicitly stated full vector-gradient formula. Exponents 2 − n and 1 − n are real subtraction, not truncated natural subtraction.
constant_dependencies: There are no existential constants, normalization factors, or unspecified bounds. F depends on n and x through the displayed dimension branch and norm. Sphere values and radial derivatives depend only on n and R. The coefficients and exponents are exactly those displayed: 1/R for n = 2, and coefficient 2 − n with exponents 2 − n and 1 − n for n ≥ 3.
